## Results

Non-Hermitian phase transitions with transfer matrix
The sketch, illustrating both the optical and acoustic components, is presented in Fig. 1. The optical portion illustrates the method by which the CNT film is stimulated by a 532 nm pulsed laser. The CNT film has recently emerged as a groundbreaking platform for achieving acoustic gain in a highly controllable manner36, with significant potential for advancing acoustic devices that facilitate efficient photo-thermo-acoustic energy conversions33,37. Its ultrathin profile renders it acoustically transparent (Supplementary Note 1), allowing sound waves to propagate freely in the transverse direction with minimal impact on wave transmission, a feature distinct from conventional electromechanical loudspeakers that exhibit high levels of reflection. Consequently, the CNT film holds great promise for integration into acoustic non-Hermitian systems (Supplementary Note 2).

In the acoustic portion illustrated in Fig. 1, we consider a waveguide that supports plane wave propagation within the operation frequency range k0A < 2\pi, where A represents the side length of the waveguide cross-section, k0 = \omega/c0 is the wave number, \omega is the angular frequency, and c0 is the sound velocity in air. By introducing a pair of loss (sponge) and gain (CNT film) material, the system becomes non-Hermitian; however, the propagation for the acoustic pressure p can still be described by the one-dimensional (1D) Helmholtz equation. We decompose the pressure field outside the photoacoustic non-Hermitian system into the forward wave (denoted by “+”) and backward wave (denoted by “−”). As such, p+ and p− represent the sound pressure spreading along the forward and backward directions, respectively, originating from the loss and gain sides.

The scattering matrix Sr, which describes the relationship between incoming and outgoing acoustic waves in the 1D system, can be expressed as:

[p+L, p−G]T = Sr [p−L, p+G]T = [S11 S12; S21 S22] [p−L, p+G]T, (1)

where S11 (S22) represents the reflection coefficient from the loss (gain) side and S21 (S12) represents the transmission coefficient. Due to the transmission reciprocity, we have S12 = S21. Sr can be calculated using a transmission-matrix approach:

S11 = (u\Gamma2 + i\Lambda2 eix)/\Delta,
S22 = (u\Gamma1 + i\Lambda2 e−ix)/\Delta,
S12 = S21 = 2/\Delta, (2)

where \Delta = −u\Gamma1 + 2cosy + i\Lambda1 eix, x = k0d, and ks = \omega/\rho s = \kappa s is the wavenumber in the loss medium. \rho s and \kappa s denote the mass density and bulk modulus of the loss material, respectively. Both of them can be retrieved from the experimentally measured Sr by a parameter extraction algorithm at any operating frequency38. The variables \Gamma1, \Gamma2, \Lambda1, and \Lambda2 are all intermediate variables with respect to coupling d. Additionally, u = −YCNT/Y0 denotes the complex admittance ratio between the assembled CNT film (Supplementary Note 3) and background medium air, which can be precisely adjusted by a pulsed laser. In this model, the loss medium is a conventional bulk material (porous sponge) with a defined width D, whereas the gain medium is a piece of CNT film with negligible thickness. The geometrically asymmetric unit described in Eq. (2) exhibits reciprocity and linearity, allowing different types of EPs to emerge through the tuning of coupling d (Supplementary Note 4).

For instance, S11 = 0 (the blue curve in Fig. 2) describes a reflectionless phenomenon when waves come from the loss side, which can be observed at any coupling d by adjusting the equivalent admittance (u = −i\Lambda2 eix/\Gamma2) of the assembled CNT film. Thus, the transmission evolves to S12 = 2/\Gamma2, and its amplitude can be modulated to 1 at a coupling of d = 5.31 cm with u = 0.456 + i0.257 [see the top maps in Fig. 2a, c]. This scattering property bears resemblance to the loss-side invisibility observed at the EP in PT-symmetric systems. Notably, while the reflection from the gain side remain high in a PT-symmetric system operating at this EP14,15, the reflection from the gain side in our system is minimal [see the top map in Fig. 2b] due to the continuous interactions.

Furthermore, this setup also allows for the realization of the less commonly mentioned reversed invisibility EP in PT-symmetric systems. Similarly, the red curve in Fig. 2 represents the reflectionless phenomenon S22 = 0 from the gain side. Thus, the admittance of the CNT film is given by u = −i\Lambda2 e−ix/\Gamma1. Building upon this, the gain-side invisibility EP occurs when the amplitude of the transmission coefficient |S12| = 1/|\Gamma1| equals 1 at d = 4.34 cm with u = 0.435 + i0.291 [see the middle maps in Fig. 2b, c].

Our system, by tuning the relevant parameters d and u, is also able to achieve bidirectional scattering properties at the EP of anti-PT symmetry, where S*11 = S22 and Im(S12) = 0. When focusing on the orange curve and the six bottom maps with d = 3.88 cm and u = 0.657 + i0.24 in Fig. 2, several observations can be made: first, |S11| = |S22| in Fig. 2a, b; second, Arg(S11) = −Arg(S22) in Fig. 2d, e; and third, Arg(S12) = 0 in Fig. 2f. It should be noted that while we have implemented the EP of an anti-PT-symmetric system through the intrinsic scattering matrix, our system does not need to satisfy the condition of balanced gain and loss in the traditional sense, as the LIT-induced gain can be tuned independently. In addition, the PT symmetry and anti-PT symmetry can be generated depending on the coupling d and the laser parameters, as discussed in Notes 5 and 6.

Non-Hermitian phase transitions using LIT
In a prior study39, we effectively showcased acoustic gain through electro-thermal-acoustic effects. Expanding on this investigation, here we present the construction of an experimental system based on LIT and establish that PT-symmetric phase transitions can be achieved within a unified device through the manipulation of coupling d. In our configuration, the CNT film functions as a bidirectional acoustic transparent medium. This means that the change in sound pressure and medium velocity across the film is minimal, resulting in negligible impedance mismatch. Additionally, we deliberately set the specific sound pressure amplitude ratio and phase difference between the sound wave generated by the CNT film and the sound source. Consequently, the overall scattering matrix Sr can be derived as (see Supplementary Note 7 for details):

rL = m1 ei\phi1 ts e−ix + rs,
tL = m1 ei\phi1 ts e−ix + ts e−ix,
rG = m2 ei\phi2 rs e−i2x + 1 + rs e−i2x,
tG = m2 ei\phi2 ts e−ix + ts e−ix, (3)

Here, m1 (m2) and \phi1 (\phi2) represent the amplitude ratio and phase difference of sound pressure between the assembled CNT film and the sound source when the incident wave comes from the loss (gain) side, respectively; rs and ts represent the reflection and transmission coefficients of the assembled loss material. It is worth noting that the nonreciprocal transmission phenomenon described by the 2nd and 3rd equations in Eq. (3) originates from the introduction of the CNT film, which provides abundant possibilities to manipulate the scattering properties in our configuration. In fact, our system retains sufficient degrees of freedom to convert from transmission nonreciprocity to reciprocity, and this can be achieved effectively by adjusting the geometric and laser parameters. For illustration, all controllable parameters in this study fulfill the premise of transmission reciprocity, specifically tL = tG = t. Based on this foundation, we emphasize the importance of judiciously optimizing the contrast ratio (m1 and m2), the coupling d, and the phases (including \phi1 and \phi2) in our system.

To gain a deeper understanding of these unusual scattering responses, we analyze the scattering spectra and eigenvalues of the system’s scattering matrix, as shown in Fig. 3 as functions of coupling d. Figure 3a–c demonstrates the existence of an EP where loss-side invisibility occurs, characterized by parameters m1 = 0.262, \phi1 = −0.91, m2 = 0.335, and \phi2 = 0.942. At a coupling of d = 5.31 cm, the reflection coefficient at the loss side (rL) is zero, indicating a sudden phase change in reflection. Meanwhile, the reflection at the gain side is nonzero with rG = 0.555ei1.237, which indicates the unidirectional reflectionless characteristics in opposite directions and highlighting the unidirectional scattering properties of the photoacoustic non-Hermitian bianisotropic system.

On the other hand, the experimental results demonstrating the anti-PT-symmetric EP of bidirectional conjugated reflections and pure real transmission are shown in Fig. 4e, f. Consistent with the simulation curves, both the bidirectional reflection amplitudes and transmission amplitudes intersect at f0 = 6 kHz in Fig. 4e. Additionally, the bidirectional reflection phases are opposite to each other, while the transmission phases are close to 0 in Fig. 4f. More specifically, the measured scattering matrix at the EP is rL = 0.578ei0.401, tL = 1.256e−i0.02, rG = 0.567e−i0.405, and tG = 1.239e−i0.01, illustrating the EP behavior of the anti-PT-symmetric system.

Formation of acoustic VBs and scattering EP using LIT
The LIT method employed in this study represents a promising approach for achieving perfect acoustic VBs and enables the PT-symmetric scattering behavior illustrated in Fig. 5a. In the aforementioned configuration, the CNT film under laser irradiation functions effectively as a point sound source, since the timescale of laser-induced heat diffusion across the film surface is on the order of seconds40. When the laser spot rotates on the CNT film at a modulation frequency of fr (e.g., fr = 0.1 kHz), the diffusion time is much longer than the rotation period, ensuring that the acoustic source rotates continuously rather than discretely. As a result, the system produces perfect acoustic VBs within the waveguide, unlike the approximate VBs generated by discrete passive41 or electronical driven35 methods. This continuous, contact-free excitation is a defining advantage of LIT and fundamentally differentiates it from previous electrical approaches.

The physical mechanism and spatial distribution of the acoustic VB generated by a rotating laser spot are discussed in Supplementary Note 10. To support the propagation of first-order VBs, the waveguide was replaced with a cylindrical tube of radius R0 = 2 cm. A schematic of the LIT-generated VB is shown in Fig. 5b, in which a certain angle is set between the symmetry axis of the reflector and the rotation axis of the motor, causing the laser to trace a circular trajectory on the CNT film. Supplementary Movies 1 and 2 demonstrate the laser spot rotating on the CNT film to form a circular trajectory at rotational speeds of 150 revolutions per minute (RPM) and 6000 RPM, respectively. The corresponding simulation and experimental results, after Fourier transformation, are presented in Fig. 5c, d, confirming that the LIT system produces a stable and well-defined acoustic VB (details in Supplementary Note 11).

To understand the scattering behavior of VBs at the EP, we modeled the scattering responses for counter-clockwise (CCW) vortex excitations (see Supplementary Note 12), with the corresponding scattering matrices revealing distinct symmetry-breaking features inherent to non-Hermitian systems:

Sr = [rL tL; tL rG] = [rL1 tL1; tL1 rG1] + [rL2 tL2; tL2 rG2] (6)

where the scattering coefficients represent only the normalized ratios between the reflected or transmitted pressure amplitudes and that of the incident wave. These quantities are independent of the vortex topological charge itself; the charge merely determines the rotational phase structure of the field.

Figure 5e, f demonstrated the simulated and experimentally measured scattering amplitudes and phases of the acoustic CCW VBs at the operating frequency of f0 = 6 kHz and rotation frequency of fr = 0.1 kHz, respectively. The corresponding CW characteristics are shown in Fig. 5h, i. The data reveal a remarkable behavior: when a CCW VB is incident from the loss side, the reflected VB is suppressed (rL = 0), and the transmitted VB preserves its amplitude but reverses its topological charge relative to the incident wave. In contrast, when the VB is incident from the gain side, the transmitted mode remains reversed (tG = −eiy), while the reflected field becomes a superposition of two VBs with distinct topological charges, rG = rG1 + rG2 = −ei2y/s−2 (see Supplementary Note 13 for details). Here, s is the complex reflection/transmission coefficient of the loss medium with rs = ts = s = |s|ei\alpha; |s| and \alpha are the amplitude and phase.

A more intuitive visualization is provided in Fig. 5g, j, showing the measured cross-sectional field distributions of CCW and CW VBs with a coupling d = 9.92 cm, corresponding to the vertical dashed lines in Fig. 5e, f, h, i, respectively. The fitted CNT film parameters for this EP are m11 = 1, \phi11 = \pi; m12 = 0, \phi12 = 0; m21 = 1, \phi21 = \pi; and m22 = 1/|s|, \phi22 = \pi−\alpha. The experimentally obtained scattering coefficients are rL1 = 0.068ei0.619, tL1 = 0.069ei0.57, rG1 = 1.811e−i1.803, tG1 = 0.015ei0.615, rL2 = 0.327ei0.181, tL2 = 1.016e−i3.102, rG2 = 1.982e−i3.015, and tG2 = 0.997e−i3.1 at the azimuth angle of \theta = 0. These results collectively confirm the realization of PT-symmetric scattering with acoustic VBs and the experimental observation of topological charge reversal at the EP. This finding represents the first experimental demonstration of PT symmetry in acoustic VBs, marking a substantial advance in non-Hermitian acoustics. The LIT platform not only enables the study of symmetry breaking in structured acoustic fields but also establishes a versatile route for exploring topological effects and non-Hermitian phase transitions beyond plane-wave systems.

## Methods

Loss measurement
In order to verify the universality of this methodology, a common sponge sheet was selected as the acoustic loss material in our experiments. In the plane wave scenario, the measured reflection and transmission coefficients of the loss at 6 kHz are rs = 0.213ei0.585 and ts = 0.815e−i2.093. A standard extraction algorithm is used to retrieve the effective parameters of the sponge from the measured scattering matrix38. In our prototype sample, the mass density of surrounding background medium (air) is \rho0 = 1.21 kg/m3 and the bulk modulus is \kappa0 = 0.142 MPa. Thus, the retrieved mass density and bulk modulus are \rho s = 1.339ei0.144 kg/m3 and \kappa s = 0.177ei0.342 MPa, respectively. On the other hand, in the acoustic VB scenario, the reflection and transmission coefficients of the loss (thickness D = 0.4 cm) at 6.1 kHz are rs = ts = 0.559e−i1.137, and the retrieved mass density and bulk modulus are \rho s = 2.236e−i.249 kg/m3 and \kappa s = 0.12e−i0.444 MPa, respectively.

Active gain design
A CNT film irradiated by pulsed laser is used to achieve an artificial acoustic gain material since no passive acoustic gain material exists in nature. The film is placed inside the waveguide vertically and hence radiates plane waves (or VBs) facing opposite directions with identical amplitude and initial phase when pumped by laser. We control the effective transmission and reflection of the artificial CNT film to generate the predesigned effective gain medium.

Full-wave simulations
The simulations are performed by the full-wave finite element solver COMSOL Multiphysics, through which we validate these unusual scattering responses and obtain in-depth physical insights into the operation of this device. The pressure acoustic module and the acoustic heat source domain are used so that both loss and CNT can be fully modeled for this multi-physics process. The calculation domain is terminated by radiation boundary conditions that also include the incident field.

Comment P1.5 – Is electro-thermoacoustic method with CNT film feasible for this concept?
What’s the advantage of the LIT technology?
Response: The reviewer has brought up a valuable point about the feasibility and advantages of
the LIT technology, which deserves to be carefully clarified. The electro-thermoacoustic method is
indeed feasible for the proposed concept, and it offers distinct advantages. This method, which requires
two input signals, is particularly effective when compared to traditional electromagnetic loudspeakers.
Preliminary experiments using the electro-thermoacoustic approach [Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 066601
(2023); Adv. Mater. 36, 2406567 (2024)] have already demonstrated its practical viability.
However, the LIT technology offers unique benefits that set it apart from conventional methods.
One of the key advantages of LIT is that it operates without the need for physical contact, electrical
connections, or magnetic fields, unlike the electro-thermoacoustic approach, which requires additional
control and power circuitry. This contactless nature makes LIT particularly advantageous in complex or
constrained environments, where minimizing setup complexity is crucial. Furthermore, LIT technology
is more energy-efficient than electrical methods. In the case of LIT, almost the entire optical energy
is converted into phonon populations due to the photoacoustic effect, which is driven by inter-cone
transitions in the Dirac band structure of graphene. This results in a photon-wavelength-independent
absorption coefficient across the visible range. The dominant electronic cooling mechanism is non-
radiative electron–phonon scattering at these wavelengths, as demonstrated in previous work [Nat.
Mater. 10, 569 (2011)]. Additionally, studies have shown that LIT works effectively both in air and
liquid without significant degradation of the structure [Nano Lett. 8, 4539 (2010)].

the apparent discrepancy between the description of multiple interferences in the loss–gain unit and the

The three idiosyncratic EPs indeed arise from multiple interferences occurring within the loss–gain
unit, as described in the last paragraph of the Introduction Section. These interferences capture the

non-Hermitian behavior of the system. While the transfer matrix method is typically used to describe
the scattering properties of the entire system, it treats each component as an effective element with-

macroscopic description of system behavior, whereas the multiple-interference approach offers a micro-
scopic view of the internal energy exchanges between the coupled subsystems. Despite this difference in
perspective, the two approaches are fully consistent and complementary. Both ultimately describe the
same physical process—the propagation, reflection, and transmission of acoustic waves through a cou-
pled non-Hermitian structure—and lead to identical scattering characteristics. In this sense, the TMM
and multiple-interference descriptions are equivalent in representing the global response of the system
and its corresponding EPs. To address the reviewer’s concerns, we construct a physical model and
determine the EPs of the three observed modes within the multiple-interference framework, which

Comment P1.7 – In the manuscript, the scattering EP means the EPs of the scattering matrix.
Could the authors provide a more intuitive picture of the scattering EPs? Maybe compared to EPs
of a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful remark and agree that the non-Hermitian Hamilto-
nian offers an intuitive framework for understanding EPs, particularly in cavity-coupled PT-symmetric
systems where intrinsic resonance frequencies are well-defined. This approach has been widely applied
in both optical systems [Science 373, 1261 (2021)] and acoustic systems [Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 066601
(2023)], providing clear insights into phase transitions. However, our study adopts a different approach
that does not rely on resonance modes defined by a Hamiltonian. Instead, we focus on the scatter-
ing process, where multiple interactions between the PT-symmetric bulk loss and internal admittance
shape the reflected and transmitted waves, giving rise to scattering EPs. This method contrasts with
the more conventional Hamiltonian-based models but still captures the essence of non-Hermitian phase
transitions. In the context of scatterer-based PT-symmetric systems, significant discoveries such as
negative reflection [Phys. Rev. Lett. 113, 023903 (2014)] and impurity immunity [Phys. Rev. X 8,
031035 (2018)] have demonstrated the potential of scattering EPs. The scattering matrix approach
offers an alternative to the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, particularly in systems where resonance modes
are less prominent or absent.
emphasizes the role of sound amplitudes and phases in describing the scattering properties of the sys-
tem. While non-Hermitian Hamiltonian EPs primarily describe internal dynamics (e.g., eigenmodes),
our scattering EPs are directly linked to the macroscopic behavior of the system, providing a clearer
picture of the phase transitions as observed experimentally. Our theoretical models, simulations, and
experimental results are in strong agreement, further validating our approach. Nevertheless, we appreci-
ate the reviewer’s suggestion to explore the use of an effective Hamiltonian method for scatterer-based
systems and will carefully consider its potential application in future work.

and the observation of non-Hermitian phase transitions. The system is modeled using the transfer-

Response: We would like to express our sincere gratitude to the reviewer for the careful evaluation of
our manuscript and for the positive recognition of its clarity, structure, and self-consistent results. We
are grateful for the reviewer’s thoughtful comments and constructive suggestions, which have helped
us refine the manuscript and strengthen the presentation of our findings. In the following, we provide
detailed responses and corresponding revisions addressing each of the reviewer’s concerns.
Comment P2.2 – The physics of PT symmetry, EPs and anti-PT symmetry has been well
studied in various contexts. Even for acoustics, anti-PT symmetry has been studied by some of the
authors (see PRL 131, 066601 (2023)). The physical phenomena in the present work are not new.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this important point, which allows us to clarify
the novelty and fundamental distinctions of our work from previous studies, particularly Ref. 28 (Phys.
Rev. Lett. 131, 066601 (2023)). Although our research shares conceptual ground in exploring PT
symmetry, EPs, and anti-PT symmetry, the underlying physical mechanisms, theoretical frameworks,
and experimental implementations are entirely different.
Unlike Ref. 28, which investigates a cavity-tube system modeled as a topological SSH chain
using a tight-binding Hamiltonian, our study is based on a scattering system described through the
transfer matrix formalism derived from transmission-line theory. The cavity-tube model focuses on
the intrinsic modal properties of coupled resonators, where PT-symmetry breaking is expressed through
eigenvalue coalescence in the Hamiltonian spectrum. In contrast, our work examines the extrinsic
scattering behavior of acoustic waves, where PT and anti-PT symmetries manifest through reflection
and transmission characteristics governed by the spatial distribution of gain and loss.
This distinction is further exemplified in the anti-PT case. In Ref. 28, anti-PT symmetry arises
from the coupling of eigenmodes within the Hamiltonian framework, reflecting internal energy dynam-
ics. In our system, however, anti-PT symmetry is observed directly in the scattering response, where
conjugate reflection and purely real transmission coexist under wave excitation—an experimentally ver-
ifiable signature distinct from the internal energy distribution reported previously. To the best of our
knowledge, this represents the first experimental realization of such conjugate reflection and real-valued
transmission in an acoustic anti-PT configuration.
Beyond the conventional PT and anti-PT regimes, our system also supports a reversed-PT-
symmetric phase, a phenomenon rarely reported in acoustics. This state occurs when the system
is excited from the gain side, yet it still exhibits unidirectional transparency—a reversal of the usual
PT scattering behavior, where excitation from the loss side leads to transparency. The realization of
reversed-PT symmetry underscores the versatility of our laser-induced thermoacoustic (LIT) platform,
10
whichallowsprecisecontrolofgain–lossinteractionsandfielddistribution,capabilitiesdifficulttoachieve
with traditional loudspeaker-based or cavity-coupled systems.
A key strength of our approach lies in its integration of PT, reversed-PT, and anti-PT sym-
metries within a single unified experimental system. To our knowledge, this is the first time these
distinct non-Hermitian phase transitions and their mutual conversions have been experimentally realized
together. While our current focus is on plane-wave excitations, the same principle can be extended
to arbitrary acoustic wavefronts, including PT-symmetric acoustic vortices, which are discussed in the
subsequentsection. Thisunifiedframeworknotonlydemonstratesthecoexistenceofmultiplesymmetry
regimes but also provides a flexible foundation for designing advanced acoustic devices with reconfig-
urable non-Hermitian functionalities.
In light of this clarification, we have revised the relevant description in the manuscript on Page 2
as: “Nevertheless, due to the absence of an efficient experimental methodology, the establishment of
an acoustic anti-PT-symmetric configuration remains exceedingly rare, hindering the phase transitions
between PT and anti-PT symmetries within a single unified system—a challenge exacerbated by the
incompatible forms of coupling leading to their anti-communication. Although studies on PT phase
transitions, including those of anti-PT symmetry, in cavity-tube systems simulating tight-binding mod-
els have been reported [28], the anti-PT phase transitions in scattering systems remain a topic worthy
of further investigation.”
Comment P2.3 – The experimental implementation is also similar to what has been established
by some of the authors. In their previous papers (see Nature 597, 655 (2021) and PRL 131, 066601
(2023)), the acoustic gain was also provided by a carbon nanotube film driven electronically (here
the carbon nanotube film is driven by a laser).
Response: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful observation. It is true that both our present
laser-driven approach and the previously reported electrically driven method [Nature 597, 655 (2021);
Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 066601 (2023)] utilize CNT films as non-Hermitian acoustic gain elements. From
a physical standpoint, both mechanisms share the same fundamental origin: the rapid electron–phonon
relaxation process following carrier excitation increases the lattice temperature of the CNT film, gener-
ating thermal waves that are subsequently transferred to the surrounding air. The resulting expansion
of the adjacent air layers acts as an acoustic piston, producing sound radiation.
Although the underlying thermoacoustic principle is common, the driving mechanisms and re-
sulting acoustic behaviors differ profoundly. In the electrically driven configuration, the CNT film
is excited by alternating current, leading to periodic Joule heating. The generated acoustic signal is
typically at twice the driving frequency, with the waveform determined by the uniform resistive heating
profile of the film. This approach is well suited for producing geometrically defined sound fields—for
instance, cylindrical wavefronts when the film is wrapped around a tubular substrate, as demonstrated
in Nature 597, 655 (2021).
In contrast, the laser-pumped configuration adopted in this study is contactless, electrically and
magnetically passive, and free from external wiring or circuitry, which greatly simplifies system in-
tegration, especially in confined or high-interference environments. Beyond practicality, laser excitation
offers significant physical advantages. Nearly all absorbed optical energy contributes to phonon genera-
tion due to the wavelength-independent optical absorption of graphene-based CNTs and the dominance
ofnon-radiativeelectron–phononscattering[Nat. Mater. 10,569(2011)]. Thisresultsinhigherconver-
11
sion efficiency compared to electrical pumping. Furthermore, CNT films maintain excellent mechanical
and thermal stability in both air and liquid environments without structural degradation [Nano Lett. 8,
4539 (2010)].
A particularly important distinction lies in the diversity of acoustic waveforms accessible under
laser excitation. Because the characteristic thermal diffusion time of the CNT film (on the order of 10
cm2 area in this work) is much longer than the acoustic period, spatiotemporal modulation of the laser
beamcandynamicallyshapetheemittedsoundfield. Forinstance, whenthelaserspotisrotatedaround
the central axis of the waveguide and at a frequency such as f = 0.1 kHz on the film, the continuous
r
heating trajectory gives rise to a stable, coherent acoustic vortex beam (VB) within the waveguide.
This continuous rotation produces a genuine vortex field, as opposed to the discrete vortex-like struc-
tures previously realized using passive [Phys. Rev. Lett. 117, 034301 (2016)] or electrically driven
[Adv. Mater. 34, 202202026 (2022)] configurations. To verify this effect, as a proof-of-concept, we
developed theoretical models and performed experiments demonstrating the generation of a first-order
acoustic vortex beam under rotating laser excitation. This result highlights the unique capabilities of
laser-induced thermoacoustics for achieving controllable, broadband, and geometrically versatile sound
fields—capabilities unattainable with the earlier electrically driven CNT systems.
(1) Theoretical models for acoustic vortex beams realized by laser-induced thermoacoustics
The method employed in this work—laser-induced thermoacoustics (LIT)—provides a simpler and
more efficient alternative to the electrically driven CNT films used in previous studies. While previous
research (Nature 597, 655, 2021; Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 066601, 2023) has demonstrated acoustic gain
through CNT films driven electrically, our approach harnesses the unique properties of laser excitation,
eliminating the need for complex electronic circuit designs. For example, the generation of acoustic VBs
can be accomplished by simply introducing a rotating laser beam, which induces a rotational Doppler
effect. This stands in contrast to the more intricate methods required for electrically pumped CNT film
systems.

From a physics perspective, this study reports the first experimental realization of non-Hermitian
phase transitions in an open scattering system. Unlike our previous work [Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 066601
(2023)], which described non-Hermitian behavior within a closed cavity-tube network modeled by an
effective Hamiltonian, the current system is formulated directly through scattering matrices belong-
ing to the PT-symmetric family. This distinction is fundamental: the present approach captures the
full wave dynamics of an open system, revealing three distinct symmetry regimes—PT, reversed-PT,
and anti-PT—that have not been observed together in a single experimental platform. While each
symmetry has been discussed separately in earlier theoretical reports, our experiments demonstrate their
coexistenceandthetransitionsbetweenthem,includingthemaskingandunmaskingprocessesnearEPs.
This comprehensive observation of symmetry transitions establishes a new experimental framework for
exploring non-Hermitian physics in scattering systems.
In terms of experimental methodology, our approach represents a major step beyond the electri-
cally driven CNT film systems used in earlier studies [Nature 597, 655 (2021)]. Electrically driven CNT
films were limited by electrode configurations and thermal diffusion, constraining the spatial flexibility
of sound generation. In contrast, the laser-induced thermoacoustic (LIT) platform developed here en-
ables non-contact, programmable, and broadband acoustic excitation. For instance, by rotating a laser
beam across the CNT film, we can dynamically sculpt the spatial phase of the generated acoustic fields,
producing vortex beams with well-defined topological charges. This capability not only enhances exper-
imental controllability but also makes it possible to realize non-Hermitian phase transitions for arbitrary
wavefronts, extending beyond the plane-wave configurations that dominated previous PT studies. The
successful observation of an EP associated with an acoustic vortex beam marks, to our knowledge, the
first such demonstration in acoustics.
To address the reviewer’s concern and provide a clear proof-of-concept, we further modeled the
quasi-PT-symmetric scattering behavior of vortex beams at the exceptional point, simulating and ex-
perimentally confirming the phase transitions induced by CCW vortex incidence (m = 1). The corre-
sponding scattering matrices for both CCW and CW vortex excitations are presented, revealing distinct
symmetry-breaking behaviors. Furthermore, we derived the parameter conditions for achieving unidi-
rectional transparency and experimentally observed the reversal of the transmitted beam’s topological
charge—an effect that directly evidences non-Hermitian topology in vortex-field space.

represents a promising approach for achieving perfect acoustic VBs and enables the PT-symmetric
scattering behavior illustrated in Fig. 5(a). In the aforementioned configuration, the CNT film under
laser irradiation functions effectively as a point sound source, since the timescale of laser-induced heat
diffusion across the film surface is on the order of seconds [40]. When the laser spot rotates on the
CNT film at a modulation frequency of f (e.g., f = 0.1 kHz), the diffusion time is much longer than
r r
the rotation period, ensuring that the acoustic source rotates continuously rather than discretely. As
a result, the system produces perfect acoustic VBs within the waveguide, unlike the approximate VBs
generated by discrete passive [41] or electronical driven [35] methods. This continuous, contact-free
excitation is a defining advantage of LIT and fundamentally differentiates it from previous electrical
approaches.

Comment P2.5 – Another technique issue: the symmetry operators were not given in the text.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. The clarification regarding
symmetry operators is indeed important, as it helps to distinguish between the different theoretical
frameworks used to describe non-Hermitian acoustic systems. In the field of PT-symmetric acoustics,
existing research can generally be divided into two main categories: the cavity-tube model and the
scattering model. The cavity-tube model, as discussed for example in [Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 066601
(2023)], focuses on the intrinsic resonant modes of coupled cavities. In this framework, the system is

## Paper

## Abstract

Non-Hermitian physics in open systems has garnered significant attention for its exotic phenomena, particularly surrounding exceptional points that offer transformative potential for multifunctional devices. Central to this field are parity-time (PT) symmetry-defined by balanced gain and loss-and its counterpart, anti-PT symmetry. However, integrating these divergent concepts into a unified acoustic platform remains an unattainable challenge. In this study, we employ laser-induced thermoacoustics (LIT) to integrate a tunable amplifying component into a non-Hermitian system. By exciting an ultrathin carbon nanotube (CNT) film through laser irradiation, we experimentally observe the phase transitions between PT and anti-PT symmetries. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate the creation of selectable scattering states and the generation of acoustic vortex beams (VBs), facilitating both PT-symmetric scattering and the conversion of topological charges. This acoustically transparent strategy bypasses traditional, path-blocking compensation schemes, offering a versatile framework for controlled non-Hermitian phase transitions in next-generation integrated devices.

---

## Introduction

One of the most intriguing advancements in quantum mechanics over recent decades has been the discovery of non-Hermitian Hamiltonian H that commutes with the parity-time (PT) operator, leading to the emergence of real-energy eigenvalues1. This finding has sparked significant interest in exploring its classical counterpart across various domains, with applications in photonics2–11, acoustics12–21, and beyond22–24, by utilizing balanced gain-loss regions. Anti-PT-symmetric non-Hermitian systems, serving as the conjugate counterparts, have expanded the realm of non-Hermitian symmetries and have been experimentally realized through spatially coupled flying atom beams25, electrical circuits26, and optical waveguides featuring imaginary couplings27. Nevertheless, due to the absence of an efficient experimental methodology, the establishment of an acoustic anti-PT-symmetric configuration remains exceedingly rare, hindering the phase transitions between PT and anti-PT symmetries within a single unified system-a challenge exacerbated by the incompatible forms of coupling leading to their anti-communication. Although studies on PT phase transitions, including those of anti-PT symmetry, in cavity-tube systems simulating tight-binding models have been reported28, the anti-PT phase transitions in scattering systems remain a topic worthy of further investigation.

The crucial factor in achieving the phase transition between acoustic PT and anti-PT symmetries lies in identifying dependable and controllable acoustic gain medium. While in photonics, gain can be readily induced through stimulated emission via optical or electrical excitation from an external source, or through parametric processes29–31, the realm of acoustics faces challenges. The implementation of PT symmetry in experimental configurations typically necessitates the utilization of piezoelectric transducers32, electromechanical cone loudspeakers13,14, or forced air flows16, as natural passive acoustic gain materials are absent. These mechanically-driven acoustic gain strategies present significant practical hurdles and impose constraints on achieving controlled PT symmetry due to substantial impedance mismatches with the ambient air and the inherent rigidity, leading to limited adaptability.

Nonetheless, a newer related technology, laser-induced thermoacoustics (LIT), which leverages pulsed laser light to generate acoustic waves through rapid thermal expansion may be a candidate approach for acoustic gain. This process involves three primary steps: absorption, thermal expansion, and acoustic wave generation33. In medical imaging, this principle is used in photoacoustic imaging, where specific wavelengths are chosen to target particular tissues or chromophores such as hemoglobin and melanin, enhancing contrast and providing detailed images of biological structures34. The characteristics of the generated sound waves, such as their frequency and amplitude, depend on the properties of the material and the parameters of the laser pulse, including its duration, wavelength, and intensity. This non-invasiveness is beneficial in both medical and material testing applications, where preserving the integrity of the subject is crucial. In addition, active methods for generating acoustic VB have been reported in ref. 35, and LIT may provide a viable alternative approach.

In this study, we propose a general methodology to access the complex coupling by modulating the non-Hermitian system and further facilitate the phase transitions between PT and anti-PT symmetries within a unified acoustics system using LIT. As a demonstration, we experimentally construct a compact non-Hermitian unit consisting of a pair of acoustic loss (sponge) and gain (CNT film) loaded in a waveguide. This unit provides multiple interferences in the structure when incident waves impinge on one of the components, in stark contrast to the conventional acoustic gain media like back-to-back loudspeaker pairs that absorb the incident sound field and then reradiate it14. Unlike PT-symmetric system where unidirectional reflectionless can only be demonstrated from the loss side, our method reverses the orientation at identical operating frequency. Strikingly, the proposed platform also allows for the achievement of anti-PT symmetry through the delicate interplay between gain and loss. Due to the innovation of LIT, acoustic VBs can be conveniently generated, and their PT-symmetric scattering behavior has been realized, along with the conversion of the topological charge. The combination of LIT and PT-symmetric acoustics bridges two critical aspects of non-Hermitian physics, and provides diverse routes for controlling the phase transitions of non-Hermitian Hamiltonian.

---

## Results

Non-Hermitian phase transitions with transfer matrix
The sketch, illustrating both the optical and acoustic components, is presented in Fig. 1. The optical portion illustrates the method by which the CNT film is stimulated by a 532 nm pulsed laser. The CNT film has recently emerged as a groundbreaking platform for achieving acoustic gain in a highly controllable manner36, with significant potential for advancing acoustic devices that facilitate efficient photo-thermo-acoustic energy conversions33,37. Its ultrathin profile renders it acoustically transparent (Supplementary Note 1), allowing sound waves to propagate freely in the transverse direction with minimal impact on wave transmission, a feature distinct from conventional electromechanical loudspeakers that exhibit high levels of reflection. Consequently, the CNT film holds great promise for integration into acoustic non-Hermitian systems (Supplementary Note 2).

In the acoustic portion illustrated in Fig. 1, we consider a waveguide that supports plane wave propagation within the operation frequency range k0A < 2\pi, where A represents the side length of the waveguide cross-section, k0 = \omega/c0 is the wave number, \omega is the angular frequency, and c0 is the sound velocity in air. By introducing a pair of loss (sponge) and gain (CNT film) material, the system becomes non-Hermitian; however, the propagation for the acoustic pressure p can still be described by the one-dimensional (1D) Helmholtz equation. We decompose the pressure field outside the photoacoustic non-Hermitian system into the forward wave (denoted by “+”) and backward wave (denoted by “−”). As such, p+ and p− represent the sound pressure spreading along the forward and backward directions, respectively, originating from the loss and gain sides.

The scattering matrix Sr, which describes the relationship between incoming and outgoing acoustic waves in the 1D system, can be expressed as:

[p+L, p−G]T = Sr [p−L, p+G]T = [S11 S12; S21 S22] [p−L, p+G]T, (1)

where S11 (S22) represents the reflection coefficient from the loss (gain) side and S21 (S12) represents the transmission coefficient. Due to the transmission reciprocity, we have S12 = S21. Sr can be calculated using a transmission-matrix approach:

S11 = (u\Gamma2 + i\Lambda2 eix)/\Delta,
S22 = (u\Gamma1 + i\Lambda2 e−ix)/\Delta,
S12 = S21 = 2/\Delta, (2)

where \Delta = −u\Gamma1 + 2cosy + i\Lambda1 eix, x = k0d, and ks = \omega/\rho s = \kappa s is the wavenumber in the loss medium. \rho s and \kappa s denote the mass density and bulk modulus of the loss material, respectively. Both of them can be retrieved from the experimentally measured Sr by a parameter extraction algorithm at any operating frequency38. The variables \Gamma1, \Gamma2, \Lambda1, and \Lambda2 are all intermediate variables with respect to coupling d. Additionally, u = −YCNT/Y0 denotes the complex admittance ratio between the assembled CNT film (Supplementary Note 3) and background medium air, which can be precisely adjusted by a pulsed laser. In this model, the loss medium is a conventional bulk material (porous sponge) with a defined width D, whereas the gain medium is a piece of CNT film with negligible thickness. The geometrically asymmetric unit described in Eq. (2) exhibits reciprocity and linearity, allowing different types of EPs to emerge through the tuning of coupling d (Supplementary Note 4).

For instance, S11 = 0 (the blue curve in Fig. 2) describes a reflectionless phenomenon when waves come from the loss side, which can be observed at any coupling d by adjusting the equivalent admittance (u = −i\Lambda2 eix/\Gamma2) of the assembled CNT film. Thus, the transmission evolves to S12 = 2/\Gamma2, and its amplitude can be modulated to 1 at a coupling of d = 5.31 cm with u = 0.456 + i0.257 [see the top maps in Fig. 2a, c]. This scattering property bears resemblance to the loss-side invisibility observed at the EP in PT-symmetric systems. Notably, while the reflection from the gain side remain high in a PT-symmetric system operating at this EP14,15, the reflection from the gain side in our system is minimal [see the top map in Fig. 2b] due to the continuous interactions.

Furthermore, this setup also allows for the realization of the less commonly mentioned reversed invisibility EP in PT-symmetric systems. Similarly, the red curve in Fig. 2 represents the reflectionless phenomenon S22 = 0 from the gain side. Thus, the admittance of the CNT film is given by u = −i\Lambda2 e−ix/\Gamma1. Building upon this, the gain-side invisibility EP occurs when the amplitude of the transmission coefficient |S12| = 1/|\Gamma1| equals 1 at d = 4.34 cm with u = 0.435 + i0.291 [see the middle maps in Fig. 2b, c].

Our system, by tuning the relevant parameters d and u, is also able to achieve bidirectional scattering properties at the EP of anti-PT symmetry, where S*11 = S22 and Im(S12) = 0. When focusing on the orange curve and the six bottom maps with d = 3.88 cm and u = 0.657 + i0.24 in Fig. 2, several observations can be made: first, |S11| = |S22| in Fig. 2a, b; second, Arg(S11) = −Arg(S22) in Fig. 2d, e; and third, Arg(S12) = 0 in Fig. 2f. It should be noted that while we have implemented the EP of an anti-PT-symmetric system through the intrinsic scattering matrix, our system does not need to satisfy the condition of balanced gain and loss in the traditional sense, as the LIT-induced gain can be tuned independently. In addition, the PT symmetry and anti-PT symmetry can be generated depending on the coupling d and the laser parameters, as discussed in Notes 5 and 6.

Non-Hermitian phase transitions using LIT
In a prior study39, we effectively showcased acoustic gain through electro-thermal-acoustic effects. Expanding on this investigation, here we present the construction of an experimental system based on LIT and establish that PT-symmetric phase transitions can be achieved within a unified device through the manipulation of coupling d. In our configuration, the CNT film functions as a bidirectional acoustic transparent medium. This means that the change in sound pressure and medium velocity across the film is minimal, resulting in negligible impedance mismatch. Additionally, we deliberately set the specific sound pressure amplitude ratio and phase difference between the sound wave generated by the CNT film and the sound source. Consequently, the overall scattering matrix Sr can be derived as (see Supplementary Note 7 for details):

rL = m1 ei\phi1 ts e−ix + rs,
tL = m1 ei\phi1 ts e−ix + ts e−ix,
rG = m2 ei\phi2 rs e−i2x + 1 + rs e−i2x,
tG = m2 ei\phi2 ts e−ix + ts e−ix, (3)

Here, m1 (m2) and \phi1 (\phi2) represent the amplitude ratio and phase difference of sound pressure between the assembled CNT film and the sound source when the incident wave comes from the loss (gain) side, respectively; rs and ts represent the reflection and transmission coefficients of the assembled loss material. It is worth noting that the nonreciprocal transmission phenomenon described by the 2nd and 3rd equations in Eq. (3) originates from the introduction of the CNT film, which provides abundant possibilities to manipulate the scattering properties in our configuration. In fact, our system retains sufficient degrees of freedom to convert from transmission nonreciprocity to reciprocity, and this can be achieved effectively by adjusting the geometric and laser parameters. For illustration, all controllable parameters in this study fulfill the premise of transmission reciprocity, specifically tL = tG = t. Based on this foundation, we emphasize the importance of judiciously optimizing the contrast ratio (m1 and m2), the coupling d, and the phases (including \phi1 and \phi2) in our system.

To gain a deeper understanding of these unusual scattering responses, we analyze the scattering spectra and eigenvalues of the system’s scattering matrix, as shown in Fig. 3 as functions of coupling d. Figure 3a–c demonstrates the existence of an EP where loss-side invisibility occurs, characterized by parameters m1 = 0.262, \phi1 = −0.91, m2 = 0.335, and \phi2 = 0.942. At a coupling of d = 5.31 cm, the reflection coefficient at the loss side (rL) is zero, indicating a sudden phase change in reflection. Meanwhile, the reflection at the gain side is nonzero with rG = 0.555ei1.237, which indicates the unidirectional reflectionless characteristics in opposite directions and highlighting the unidirectional scattering properties of the photoacoustic non-Hermitian bianisotropic system.

On the other hand, the experimental results demonstrating the anti-PT-symmetric EP of bidirectional conjugated reflections and pure real transmission are shown in Fig. 4e, f. Consistent with the simulation curves, both the bidirectional reflection amplitudes and transmission amplitudes intersect at f0 = 6 kHz in Fig. 4e. Additionally, the bidirectional reflection phases are opposite to each other, while the transmission phases are close to 0 in Fig. 4f. More specifically, the measured scattering matrix at the EP is rL = 0.578ei0.401, tL = 1.256e−i0.02, rG = 0.567e−i0.405, and tG = 1.239e−i0.01, illustrating the EP behavior of the anti-PT-symmetric system.

Formation of acoustic VBs and scattering EP using LIT
The LIT method employed in this study represents a promising approach for achieving perfect acoustic VBs and enables the PT-symmetric scattering behavior illustrated in Fig. 5a. In the aforementioned configuration, the CNT film under laser irradiation functions effectively as a point sound source, since the timescale of laser-induced heat diffusion across the film surface is on the order of seconds40. When the laser spot rotates on the CNT film at a modulation frequency of fr (e.g., fr = 0.1 kHz), the diffusion time is much longer than the rotation period, ensuring that the acoustic source rotates continuously rather than discretely. As a result, the system produces perfect acoustic VBs within the waveguide, unlike the approximate VBs generated by discrete passive41 or electronical driven35 methods. This continuous, contact-free excitation is a defining advantage of LIT and fundamentally differentiates it from previous electrical approaches.

The physical mechanism and spatial distribution of the acoustic VB generated by a rotating laser spot are discussed in Supplementary Note 10. To support the propagation of first-order VBs, the waveguide was replaced with a cylindrical tube of radius R0 = 2 cm. A schematic of the LIT-generated VB is shown in Fig. 5b, in which a certain angle is set between the symmetry axis of the reflector and the rotation axis of the motor, causing the laser to trace a circular trajectory on the CNT film. Supplementary Movies 1 and 2 demonstrate the laser spot rotating on the CNT film to form a circular trajectory at rotational speeds of 150 revolutions per minute (RPM) and 6000 RPM, respectively. The corresponding simulation and experimental results, after Fourier transformation, are presented in Fig. 5c, d, confirming that the LIT system produces a stable and well-defined acoustic VB (details in Supplementary Note 11).

To understand the scattering behavior of VBs at the EP, we modeled the scattering responses for counter-clockwise (CCW) vortex excitations (see Supplementary Note 12), with the corresponding scattering matrices revealing distinct symmetry-breaking features inherent to non-Hermitian systems:

Sr = [rL tL; tL rG] = [rL1 tL1; tL1 rG1] + [rL2 tL2; tL2 rG2] (6)

where the scattering coefficients represent only the normalized ratios between the reflected or transmitted pressure amplitudes and that of the incident wave. These quantities are independent of the vortex topological charge itself; the charge merely determines the rotational phase structure of the field.

Figure 5e, f demonstrated the simulated and experimentally measured scattering amplitudes and phases of the acoustic CCW VBs at the operating frequency of f0 = 6 kHz and rotation frequency of fr = 0.1 kHz, respectively. The corresponding CW characteristics are shown in Fig. 5h, i. The data reveal a remarkable behavior: when a CCW VB is incident from the loss side, the reflected VB is suppressed (rL = 0), and the transmitted VB preserves its amplitude but reverses its topological charge relative to the incident wave. In contrast, when the VB is incident from the gain side, the transmitted mode remains reversed (tG = −eiy), while the reflected field becomes a superposition of two VBs with distinct topological charges, rG = rG1 + rG2 = −ei2y/s−2 (see Supplementary Note 13 for details). Here, s is the complex reflection/transmission coefficient of the loss medium with rs = ts = s = |s|ei\alpha; |s| and \alpha are the amplitude and phase.

A more intuitive visualization is provided in Fig. 5g, j, showing the measured cross-sectional field distributions of CCW and CW VBs with a coupling d = 9.92 cm, corresponding to the vertical dashed lines in Fig. 5e, f, h, i, respectively. The fitted CNT film parameters for this EP are m11 = 1, \phi11 = \pi; m12 = 0, \phi12 = 0; m21 = 1, \phi21 = \pi; and m22 = 1/|s|, \phi22 = \pi−\alpha. The experimentally obtained scattering coefficients are rL1 = 0.068ei0.619, tL1 = 0.069ei0.57, rG1 = 1.811e−i1.803, tG1 = 0.015ei0.615, rL2 = 0.327ei0.181, tL2 = 1.016e−i3.102, rG2 = 1.982e−i3.015, and tG2 = 0.997e−i3.1 at the azimuth angle of \theta = 0. These results collectively confirm the realization of PT-symmetric scattering with acoustic VBs and the experimental observation of topological charge reversal at the EP. This finding represents the first experimental demonstration of PT symmetry in acoustic VBs, marking a substantial advance in non-Hermitian acoustics. The LIT platform not only enables the study of symmetry breaking in structured acoustic fields but also establishes a versatile route for exploring topological effects and non-Hermitian phase transitions beyond plane-wave systems.

---

## Methods

Loss measurement
In order to verify the universality of this methodology, a common sponge sheet was selected as the acoustic loss material in our experiments. In the plane wave scenario, the measured reflection and transmission coefficients of the loss at 6 kHz are rs = 0.213ei0.585 and ts = 0.815e−i2.093. A standard extraction algorithm is used to retrieve the effective parameters of the sponge from the measured scattering matrix38. In our prototype sample, the mass density of surrounding background medium (air) is \rho0 = 1.21 kg/m3 and the bulk modulus is \kappa0 = 0.142 MPa. Thus, the retrieved mass density and bulk modulus are \rho s = 1.339ei0.144 kg/m3 and \kappa s = 0.177ei0.342 MPa, respectively. On the other hand, in the acoustic VB scenario, the reflection and transmission coefficients of the loss (thickness D = 0.4 cm) at 6.1 kHz are rs = ts = 0.559e−i1.137, and the retrieved mass density and bulk modulus are \rho s = 2.236e−i.249 kg/m3 and \kappa s = 0.12e−i0.444 MPa, respectively.

Active gain design
A CNT film irradiated by pulsed laser is used to achieve an artificial acoustic gain material since no passive acoustic gain material exists in nature. The film is placed inside the waveguide vertically and hence radiates plane waves (or VBs) facing opposite directions with identical amplitude and initial phase when pumped by laser. We control the effective transmission and reflection of the artificial CNT film to generate the predesigned effective gain medium.

Full-wave simulations
The simulations are performed by the full-wave finite element solver COMSOL Multiphysics, through which we validate these unusual scattering responses and obtain in-depth physical insights into the operation of this device. The pressure acoustic module and the acoustic heat source domain are used so that both loss and CNT can be fully modeled for this multi-physics process. The calculation domain is terminated by radiation boundary conditions that also include the incident field.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

laser-induced thermoacoustics. In particular, this approach allows to facilitate their phase transitions to be dynamically tuned
by optical means in experiment, overcoming challenges related to incompatible coupling forms between PT and anti-PT
symmetries, while also ensuring that the process is fully reversible and programmable. In addition, the integration of LIT
technique with ultra-thin flexible CNT film challenges the conventional view that acoustic gain requires electro-mechanical

In this work, the authors present the design of a non-Hermitian acoustic system and the observation of non-Hermitian phase transitions. The whole structure of the manuscript is very clear and the results are self-consistent. I have the following concerns.

In their previous papers (see Nature 597, 655 (2021) and PRL 131, 066601 (2023)), the acoustic gain was also provided by a carbon nanotube film driven electronically (here the carbon nanotube film is driven by a laser).
For a paper to be considered for Nature Communications, I would expect, at least, that there is a certain level of significance either in physics or in experimental methodology.

precision acoustic sensing, imaging, and real-time environmental monitoring. This concept—now explic-
itly discussed in the Main Text—represents a key innovation distinguishing our experimental strategy
from previous approaches.

transparent nature of the proposed configuration. Specifically, we measured the transmission coefficient
of a 10 µm-thick CNT film within a waveguide, and the results, shown in Fig. R1, confirm that the

Comment P1.5 – Is electro-thermoacoustic method with CNT film feasible for this concept?
What’s the advantage of the LIT technology?
Response: The reviewer has brought up a valuable point about the feasibility and advantages of
the LIT technology, which deserves to be carefully clarified. The electro-thermoacoustic method is
indeed feasible for the proposed concept, and it offers distinct advantages. This method, which requires
two input signals, is particularly effective when compared to traditional electromagnetic loudspeakers.
Preliminary experiments using the electro-thermoacoustic approach [Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 066601
(2023); Adv. Mater. 36, 2406567 (2024)] have already demonstrated its practical viability.
However, the LIT technology offers unique benefits that set it apart from conventional methods.
One of the key advantages of LIT is that it operates without the need for physical contact, electrical
connections, or magnetic fields, unlike the electro-thermoacoustic approach, which requires additional
control and power circuitry. This contactless nature makes LIT particularly advantageous in complex or
constrained environments, where minimizing setup complexity is crucial. Furthermore, LIT technology
is more energy-efficient than electrical methods. In the case of LIT, almost the entire optical energy
is converted into phonon populations due to the photoacoustic effect, which is driven by inter-cone
transitions in the Dirac band structure of graphene. This results in a photon-wavelength-independent
absorption coefficient across the visible range. The dominant electronic cooling mechanism is non-
radiative electron–phonon scattering at these wavelengths, as demonstrated in previous work [Nat.
Mater. 10, 569 (2011)]. Additionally, studies have shown that LIT works effectively both in air and
liquid without significant degradation of the structure [Nano Lett. 8, 4539 (2010)].

Comment P1.7 – In the manuscript, the scattering EP means the EPs of the scattering matrix.
Could the authors provide a more intuitive picture of the scattering EPs? Maybe compared to EPs
of a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful remark and agree that the non-Hermitian Hamilto-
nian offers an intuitive framework for understanding EPs, particularly in cavity-coupled PT-symmetric
systems where intrinsic resonance frequencies are well-defined. This approach has been widely applied
in both optical systems [Science 373, 1261 (2021)] and acoustic systems [Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 066601
(2023)], providing clear insights into phase transitions. However, our study adopts a different approach
that does not rely on resonance modes defined by a Hamiltonian. Instead, we focus on the scatter-
ing process, where multiple interactions between the PT-symmetric bulk loss and internal admittance
shape the reflected and transmitted waves, giving rise to scattering EPs. This method contrasts with
the more conventional Hamiltonian-based models but still captures the essence of non-Hermitian phase
transitions. In the context of scatterer-based PT-symmetric systems, significant discoveries such as
negative reflection [Phys. Rev. Lett. 113, 023903 (2014)] and impurity immunity [Phys. Rev. X 8,
031035 (2018)] have demonstrated the potential of scattering EPs. The scattering matrix approach
offers an alternative to the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, particularly in systems where resonance modes
are less prominent or absent.
emphasizes the role of sound amplitudes and phases in describing the scattering properties of the sys-
tem. While non-Hermitian Hamiltonian EPs primarily describe internal dynamics (e.g., eigenmodes),
our scattering EPs are directly linked to the macroscopic behavior of the system, providing a clearer
picture of the phase transitions as observed experimentally. Our theoretical models, simulations, and
experimental results are in strong agreement, further validating our approach. Nevertheless, we appreci-
ate the reviewer’s suggestion to explore the use of an effective Hamiltonian method for scatterer-based
systems and will carefully consider its potential application in future work.

us refine the manuscript and strengthen the presentation of our findings. In the following, we provide

Comment P2.2 – The physics of PT symmetry, EPs and anti-PT symmetry has been well
studied in various contexts. Even for acoustics, anti-PT symmetry has been studied by some of the
authors (see PRL 131, 066601 (2023)). The physical phenomena in the present work are not new.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this important point, which allows us to clarify
the novelty and fundamental distinctions of our work from previous studies, particularly Ref. 28 (Phys.
Rev. Lett. 131, 066601 (2023)). Although our research shares conceptual ground in exploring PT
symmetry, EPs, and anti-PT symmetry, the underlying physical mechanisms, theoretical frameworks,
and experimental implementations are entirely different.
Unlike Ref. 28, which investigates a cavity-tube system modeled as a topological SSH chain
using a tight-binding Hamiltonian, our study is based on a scattering system described through the
transfer matrix formalism derived from transmission-line theory. The cavity-tube model focuses on
the intrinsic modal properties of coupled resonators, where PT-symmetry breaking is expressed through
eigenvalue coalescence in the Hamiltonian spectrum. In contrast, our work examines the extrinsic
scattering behavior of acoustic waves, where PT and anti-PT symmetries manifest through reflection
and transmission characteristics governed by the spatial distribution of gain and loss.
This distinction is further exemplified in the anti-PT case. In Ref. 28, anti-PT symmetry arises
from the coupling of eigenmodes within the Hamiltonian framework, reflecting internal energy dynam-
ics. In our system, however, anti-PT symmetry is observed directly in the scattering response, where
conjugate reflection and purely real transmission coexist under wave excitation—an experimentally ver-
ifiable signature distinct from the internal energy distribution reported previously. To the best of our
knowledge, this represents the first experimental realization of such conjugate reflection and real-valued
transmission in an acoustic anti-PT configuration.
Beyond the conventional PT and anti-PT regimes, our system also supports a reversed-PT-
symmetric phase, a phenomenon rarely reported in acoustics. This state occurs when the system
is excited from the gain side, yet it still exhibits unidirectional transparency—a reversal of the usual
PT scattering behavior, where excitation from the loss side leads to transparency. The realization of
reversed-PT symmetry underscores the versatility of our laser-induced thermoacoustic (LIT) platform,
10
whichallowsprecisecontrolofgain–lossinteractionsandfielddistribution,capabilitiesdifficulttoachieve
with traditional loudspeaker-based or cavity-coupled systems.
A key strength of our approach lies in its integration of PT, reversed-PT, and anti-PT sym-
metries within a single unified experimental system. To our knowledge, this is the first time these
distinct non-Hermitian phase transitions and their mutual conversions have been experimentally realized
together. While our current focus is on plane-wave excitations, the same principle can be extended
to arbitrary acoustic wavefronts, including PT-symmetric acoustic vortices, which are discussed in the
subsequentsection. Thisunifiedframeworknotonlydemonstratesthecoexistenceofmultiplesymmetry
regimes but also provides a flexible foundation for designing advanced acoustic devices with reconfig-
urable non-Hermitian functionalities.
In light of this clarification, we have revised the relevant description in the manuscript on Page 2
as: “Nevertheless, due to the absence of an efficient experimental methodology, the establishment of
an acoustic anti-PT-symmetric configuration remains exceedingly rare, hindering the phase transitions
between PT and anti-PT symmetries within a single unified system—a challenge exacerbated by the
incompatible forms of coupling leading to their anti-communication. Although studies on PT phase
transitions, including those of anti-PT symmetry, in cavity-tube systems simulating tight-binding mod-
els have been reported [28], the anti-PT phase transitions in scattering systems remain a topic worthy
of further investigation.”
Comment P2.3 – The experimental implementation is also similar to what has been established
by some of the authors. In their previous papers (see Nature 597, 655 (2021) and PRL 131, 066601
(2023)), the acoustic gain was also provided by a carbon nanotube film driven electronically (here
the carbon nanotube film is driven by a laser).
Response: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful observation. It is true that both our present
laser-driven approach and the previously reported electrically driven method [Nature 597, 655 (2021);
Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 066601 (2023)] utilize CNT films as non-Hermitian acoustic gain elements. From
a physical standpoint, both mechanisms share the same fundamental origin: the rapid electron–phonon
relaxation process following carrier excitation increases the lattice temperature of the CNT film, gener-
ating thermal waves that are subsequently transferred to the surrounding air. The resulting expansion
of the adjacent air layers acts as an acoustic piston, producing sound radiation.
Although the underlying thermoacoustic principle is common, the driving mechanisms and re-
sulting acoustic behaviors differ profoundly. In the electrically driven configuration, the CNT film
is excited by alternating current, leading to periodic Joule heating. The generated acoustic signal is
typically at twice the driving frequency, with the waveform determined by the uniform resistive heating
profile of the film. This approach is well suited for producing geometrically defined sound fields—for
instance, cylindrical wavefronts when the film is wrapped around a tubular substrate, as demonstrated
in Nature 597, 655 (2021).
In contrast, the laser-pumped configuration adopted in this study is contactless, electrically and
magnetically passive, and free from external wiring or circuitry, which greatly simplifies system in-
tegration, especially in confined or high-interference environments. Beyond practicality, laser excitation
offers significant physical advantages. Nearly all absorbed optical energy contributes to phonon genera-
tion due to the wavelength-independent optical absorption of graphene-based CNTs and the dominance
ofnon-radiativeelectron–phononscattering[Nat. Mater. 10,569(2011)]. Thisresultsinhigherconver-
11
sion efficiency compared to electrical pumping. Furthermore, CNT films maintain excellent mechanical
and thermal stability in both air and liquid environments without structural degradation [Nano Lett. 8,
4539 (2010)].
A particularly important distinction lies in the diversity of acoustic waveforms accessible under

(1) Theoretical models for acoustic vortex beams realized by laser-induced thermoacoustics
The method employed in this work—laser-induced thermoacoustics (LIT)—provides a simpler and
more efficient alternative to the electrically driven CNT films used in previous studies. While previous

at

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their insightful feedback and for highlighting the
importance of both physical significance and methodological innovation for consideration in Nature
meets these criteria in both aspects.
From a physics perspective, this study reports the first experimental realization of non-Hermitian
phase transitions in an open scattering system. Unlike our previous work [Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 066601
(2023)], which described non-Hermitian behavior within a closed cavity-tube network modeled by an
effective Hamiltonian, the current system is formulated directly through scattering matrices belong-
ing to the PT-symmetric family. This distinction is fundamental: the present approach captures the
full wave dynamics of an open system, revealing three distinct symmetry regimes—PT, reversed-PT,
and anti-PT—that have not been observed together in a single experimental platform. While each
symmetry has been discussed separately in earlier theoretical reports, our experiments demonstrate their
coexistenceandthetransitionsbetweenthem,includingthemaskingandunmaskingprocessesnearEPs.
This comprehensive observation of symmetry transitions establishes a new experimental framework for
exploring non-Hermitian physics in scattering systems.
In terms of experimental methodology, our approach represents a major step beyond the electri-
cally driven CNT film systems used in earlier studies [Nature 597, 655 (2021)]. Electrically driven CNT
films were limited by electrode configurations and thermal diffusion, constraining the spatial flexibility
of sound generation. In contrast, the laser-induced thermoacoustic (LIT) platform developed here en-
ables non-contact, programmable, and broadband acoustic excitation. For instance, by rotating a laser
beam across the CNT film, we can dynamically sculpt the spatial phase of the generated acoustic fields,
producing vortex beams with well-defined topological charges. This capability not only enhances exper-
imental controllability but also makes it possible to realize non-Hermitian phase transitions for arbitrary
wavefronts, extending beyond the plane-wave configurations that dominated previous PT studies. The
successful observation of an EP associated with an acoustic vortex beam marks, to our knowledge, the
first such demonstration in acoustics.
To address the reviewer’s concern and provide a clear proof-of-concept, we further modeled the
quasi-PT-symmetric scattering behavior of vortex beams at the exceptional point, simulating and ex-
perimentally confirming the phase transitions induced by CCW vortex incidence (m = 1). The corre-
sponding scattering matrices for both CCW and CW vortex excitations are presented, revealing distinct
symmetry-breaking behaviors. Furthermore, we derived the parameter conditions for achieving unidi-
rectional transparency and experimentally observed the reversal of the transmitted beam’s topological
charge—an effect that directly evidences non-Hermitian topology in vortex-field space.

(2) Accessing PT symmetry in acoustic vortex beams

Formation of acoustic VBs and scattering EP using LIT. The LIT method employed in this study
represents a promising approach for achieving perfect acoustic VBs and enables the PT-symmetric
scattering behavior illustrated in Fig. 5(a). In the aforementioned configuration, the CNT film under
laser irradiation functions effectively as a point sound source, since the timescale of laser-induced heat
diffusion across the film surface is on the order of seconds [40]. When the laser spot rotates on the
CNT film at a modulation frequency of f (e.g., f = 0.1 kHz), the diffusion time is much longer than
r r
the rotation period, ensuring that the acoustic source rotates continuously rather than discretely. As
a result, the system produces perfect acoustic VBs within the waveguide, unlike the approximate VBs
generated by discrete passive [41] or electronical driven [35] methods. This continuous, contact-free
excitation is a defining advantage of LIT and fundamentally differentiates it from previous electrical
approaches.

and the rotation axis of the motor, causing the laser to trace a circular trajectory on the CNT film.

Comment P2.5 – Another technique issue: the symmetry operators were not given in the text.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. The clarification regarding
symmetry operators is indeed important, as it helps to distinguish between the different theoretical
frameworks used to describe non-Hermitian acoustic systems. In the field of PT-symmetric acoustics,
existing research can generally be divided into two main categories: the cavity-tube model and the
scattering model. The cavity-tube model, as discussed for example in [Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 066601
(2023)], focuses on the intrinsic resonant modes of coupled cavities. In this framework, the system is
described by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian whose eigenvalues correspond to the resonance frequencies,
andthePT symmetryisdefinedthroughexplicitsymmetryoperatorsactingonthesystem’seigenstates.
This model is particularly effective for studying mode coalescence and internal energy exchange between
coupledresonators. Bycontrast, thescatteringmodel, asdevelopedin[Nat. Commun. 6, 5905(2015)],
emphasizes the input–output behavior of waves interacting with a PT-symmetric medium. Instead of
analyzing intrinsic modes, this approach characterizes how incident waves are reflected and transmitted
through the system. The analysis is based on the system’s transfer matrix and the resulting scattering
matrix, which encapsulate the effects of balanced gain and loss within the medium. In this framework,
the notion of PT symmetry is expressed through the spatial distribution of gain and loss, rather than
throughsymmetryoperatorsactingoneigenmodes. Consequently,theuseofexplicitsymmetryoperators
is not required for describing the underlying physics.
In summary, the cavity model focuses on the internal modal properties of a system and relies on
Hamiltonian symmetry operators to reveal PT behavior, whereas the scattering model concentrates on
the external wave dynamics governed by the transfer and scattering matrices. Our work follows the
latter framework, where symmetry arises from the balanced gain–loss configuration rather than from
operator-based transformations. For this reason, the symmetry operators are not explicitly given in the
manuscript.
